title: I’m looking to learn game dev from scratch. Where to start?
author: yuumiocupo
selftext:
Hi!

I’ve always been a gamer and interested in gaming in general, so I thought to give this a try.
I’ve been playing with generative AI in the last months, both music and images/videos. I also have mild experience as a software engineer. I mostly feel confortable with python, but I feel I wouldn’t have much trouble learning anything new.


I guess I’m totally lost on this as I’ve never even tried to jump into game development, so I have a couple of generic questions.


First of all, is it viable for a single person (or a couple maybe) to develop a game on their own? 
I’m guessing it’s not just about the setup but also maintenance, bug fixing, balance changes, efficiency (how smooth it runs)… 
It makes it a bit scary 😅


What are some good resources I should check to start to get familiar with terms and concepts?
This will probably vary a lot depending on the kind of game, but it would be great to have a general direction.


Any advice or recommendations on things I might be missing?


Thank you very much for taking the time to read/answer!

comments.author: MysteriousPepper8908
comments.body:
Modern models like Gemini 3.0 and Claude can vibe code basic 2D platformers and top-down shooters in a single prompt so you might want to start there. Just come up with a basic idea and tell it to make it, then you'll see things you would like to fix and most of the time you can just tell it what you want changed and it'll do it but if you want to understand more, you can always go into the code and if you understand programming logic, you'll probably be able to look at a function and understand more or less what it's doing and be able to adjust certain parameters to increase damage or adjust movement speed. 


This isn't the ideal way to execute a complex vision, for that you'll want to pick an engine like Unity or Godot and then work with your LLM of choice to draft an in-depth design document before committing to any serious coding then plan out the approach to developing a minimum viable product but if you're just experimenting, there's no harm in getting a feel for tings through vibe coding some spaghetti code. 


Eventually you're going to want to watch some videos on getting started with your engine of choice as learning via talking to an LLM isn't always the most efficient approach but I'd try to just get a few basic projects out before putting too much time into a complex design.

replies.author: yuumiocupo
replies.body: Thank you!! That’s good advice and probably a good way to start getting familiar with everything. I’ll give it a try

comments.author: old_el_paso
comments.body:
It's definitely viable for a solo dev to make a game; it was viable before having AI for support, so it's all the more viable now.

Python is doable, but if you want to work in a game engine, and are most comfortable in Python, I would recommend Godot. It's native scripting language, GDscript, is syntactically similar to Python, so it's pretty easy to pick up if you're familiar with Python, and you can easily make a full game relying on just that. However, the benefit is that Godot also supports C#, so you also have the opportunity to branch into that if you want. 

You'd probably have an easier time getting resources and info once you settle on an environment/engine, but in general, I wouldn't sleep on the "study and learn" setting on chat gpt. No shade to the vibe coders, but I love coding and mostly want to use AI to help me grasp concepts and learn to code for myself, instead of just having it code for me and only doing some bug fixing on my end. The study and learn setting is great for that imo; I know Gemini and Claude are generally perfered for straight code over something like chatGPT, but as far as discussing and learning concepts, study and learn chatGPT has been great imo. For example, I've recently started working on multiplayer design after focusing on single player. I've always struggled to grasp how to approach a multiplayer game in the abstract, and talking with study and learn chatGPT helped a lot in helping me grasp how to structure a multiplayer project, how to conceptualize a client-server model, etc.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
you can literally ask AI this and it can walk you through your learning steps by steps

it pretty much depends on how much automation you want

if you want auto auto, others already have mentioned the options

if you want some involvement into the process, then just prompt AI like you normally would

I think sometimes people in this sub forget that AIs are chatbots. You can pretend they are project partners or your gamedev teacher. It work pretty well either way

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
Start with learning actual gamedev, not AI. My advice would be to start with learning something like Godot or Unity.

AI can be a useful tool once you know what you're doing but if you don't it isn't going to help much and will become a crutch.
